name: Yara Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so please tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the morning loader at a large mine, bringing rock from the face to the crusher. I'm still junior, so I check the load twice before turning and ask my trainer Imani when the ground looks wrong. The cab is noisy, but I like ending a shift knowing exactly what I moved. At home Dev and I have two children in school and a mortgage, so a missed shift is never just a missed shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that the machine still needs someone in the seat. The little AI help on our shift sheets has already saved me from copying numbers twice, but nobody's offering us shorter hours for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't mind the software; I use it every day to check unfamiliar terms after my shift. I'm still the junior person on a loader, though. The mortgage isn't small just because AI stalls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the morning loader shift and use the new checklist on the tablet. I'd put a little from each pay into our repair account, because last winter the boiler bill ate almost a month of breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with that usual knot when a bill comes home. AI Plateau sounds almost like our Tuesday, except I would still like a bit more room in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of a normal day is hardest to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's judging when the load is sitting badly before you turn. My trainer, Imani, can see it from a distance; I still have to stop and check twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Dev that the repair account comes before a weekend away. The children want us at the pool this summer, and I don't want every sensible choice to sound like a refusal.

say: I'd tell the crew the **loader** still needs a driver, even if a tablet saves us a little paperwork.
I'd say the saved time should make **shifts** easier instead of quietly adding more work.
think: I use AI daily, but my **junior** standing still makes ordinary mistakes expensive for me.
I worry more about the **mortgage** and repair bills than about a breakthrough that never comes.
do: Keep taking morning **loader shifts** and checking each load before turning.
Put a small amount from each pay into the **repair account** before booking leisure trips.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with a familiar knot about household bills.
S0.quote: The mortgage isn't small just because AI stalls.
fieldNote: Yara likes tools that help her learn, but **junior standing** keeps her alert to mistakes on a large machine.
Her first financial thought is the **repair account**, shaped by a boiler bill and two children's requests.

steps.text: Keep driving morning loader shifts and checking loads before turns
Put a little from each pay into the household repair account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the planners should show the crew what the software is changing. If buying and shift plans get done by AI, I want the people who haul the rock in the room when they set new targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My driving isn't a writing job, so I might have a little time. But if dispatch gets leaner and sends more loads per hour, a junior operator can be blamed for falling behind before robots ever arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the shift representative to get the new targets in writing. I'd also try the mine's dispatch screen after hours with Imani, so I can spot a bad instruction. In its first year I'd stay on the loader unless hours were cut, then apply at the two nearby pits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious about the screen and angry at the idea of being measured by a bad route. I can learn a new display; I can't make a crowded haul road safe by tapping faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want a place in the room, but you're also learning the new system yourself. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want both. My own practice helps on tomorrow's shift, while the representative can argue about the target everyone is held to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you send an application?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two shortened pay packets would do it. The children's school costs and the mortgage don't wait for the mine to finish its trial.

say: I'd ask management to show how **AI planning** changes targets for crews on the ground.
I'd say operators need a voice before a screen decides how many **loads** are safe.
think: My driving lasts longer than office planning, but tighter **dispatch targets** could still cut my hours.
I could learn the screen quickly, yet my **junior** position leaves little room to challenge bad numbers alone.
do: Ask the shift **representative** to get revised targets in writing this month.
Practise reading the **dispatch screen** with Imani after shifts.
Apply to two nearby pits if two **pay packets** arrive short in the first year.
feel: **Curious** about the tool and angry about unsafe targets.
S1.quote: I can learn a new display; I can't make a crowded haul road safe by tapping faster.
fieldNote: Yara separates learning the screen from **collective bargaining** over targets, and sees both as immediate work.
She gives a concrete **pay threshold** for applying elsewhere, rather than promising to leave on principle.

steps.text: Ask the shift representative for written dispatch targets
Practise the mine dispatch screen with Imani after shifts
Apply to nearby pits after two shortened pay packets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could take the office planning by 2028, but someone still has to drive for a while. I would ask the mine to tell us its equipment plans plainly, not hand us a cheerful notice and a smaller roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years until capable robots is a frighteningly short runway for a beginner operator. If the loader seat goes around 2031, I'm 48, Dev and I still have a mortgage, and I can't assume another pit will hire displaced drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union branch for a meeting about redeployment this winter and apply for the mine's funded maintenance course if it opens. I'd keep working the loader while it is there. In 2029 I'd apply for maintenance trainee posts beyond this pit if dispatch hours had begun to fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one wakes me up. I can pick up tools, but I can't squeeze a five-year career change into one afternoon between school pickup and a night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the maintenance course give you that the loader doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather learn to inspect and repair equipment than wait for someone to tell me the seat is gone. I know full AGI may help with diagnosis and robots may later handle repairs too, so I can't call maintenance a safe harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children if they saw you studying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children I'm studying because the mine may need fewer drivers. I'd also tell them their school trips aren't cancelled today; we still have wages coming in.

say: I'd tell the crew that **planning jobs** could change first, while operators still have some time.
I'd ask for honest **equipment plans** and a real discussion about redeployment.
think: By the **2031 robot date**, my loader seat may disappear while the mortgage remains.
A maintenance course might widen my choices, although **AI diagnosis** and later robots could reach that work too.
do: Ask the **union branch** for a redeployment meeting this winter.
Apply for the mine's **funded maintenance course** if it opens, while continuing loader shifts.
Apply for **maintenance trainee posts** in 2029 if dispatch hours start falling.
feel: **Alarmed** by the short runway around school and shift hours.
S2.quote: Three years until capable robots is a frighteningly short runway for a beginner operator.
fieldNote: She locates the immediate risk in **office planning**, then the larger threat in the loader seat three years later.
Yara considers maintenance as an **option**, not a guaranteed refuge from full AGI and capable robots.

steps.text: Ask the union branch for a winter redeployment meeting
Apply for a funded maintenance course if the mine opens one
Apply for maintenance trainee posts in 2029 if dispatch hours fall
Keep working loader shifts while the seat remains staffed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the mine to publish a proper transition plan. AGI in 2031 could strip out planning and checking; we shouldn't pretend operators are untouched just because robots arrive closer to 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when thinking AI arrives, I could still learn another trade, but the children will be older and their costs different. By the robot date I'd be 51. The mine may retain some people to oversee machines, and as a junior I can't bank on being one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the next intake of the mine's funded maintenance course, if places exist, and keep driving while I study. I'd take the first year after 2031 to apply for inspection or trainee repair posts if my roster shrinks. Dev and I would keep paying the mortgage before adding any new loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still serious, but I can see a calendar rather than a wall. Five years gives me time to finish a course without pretending the course solves everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the mine before the robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for an actual paid position, not a certificate on its own. We have a few months of expenses saved, not years, and the mortgage carries on through training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want the mine to put in its plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid places, dates, and a way for drivers to apply before outside candidates. If they only offer a poster, I would take my certificate to another employer.

say: I'd ask for a dated **transition plan** and funded places for current operators.
I'd remind the crew that **AGI planning** changes before robots take hands-on work.
think: At **48** I can study, but by the robot date I may be competing for fewer oversight roles.
My modest savings cannot carry a long **unpaid course** alongside the mortgage.
do: Apply for the next **funded maintenance intake** if the mine offers places.
Keep driving the **loader** while studying and paying the mortgage.
Apply for paid **inspection or repair posts** after 2031 if the roster shrinks.
feel: **Serious**, but able to picture a course calendar.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to finish a course without pretending the course solves everything.
fieldNote: Yara uses the extra years to demand a **dated offer**, not a vague promise about future skills.
She is willing to leave for **paid work**, while refusing to gamble the household's short savings on an unpaid course.

steps.text: Apply for the next funded maintenance intake if places exist
Keep driving the loader and paying the mortgage while studying
Apply for paid inspection posts after 2031 if the roster shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew that ten years should be enough notice to train people properly. AGI in 2036 would take the planning desk first, and capable robots around 2039 could take the driving, so the mine ought to start paid training long before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 at the robot date. The children would be grown, which eases school costs, but it doesn't make the mortgage vanish or give me a pension I can count on. I might be able to work through a change if I start while I'm still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for funded electrical maintenance training next year, if the mine offers it, and keep operating while I qualify. After 2036 I'd apply for paid equipment inspection posts rather than wait for 2039. Dev and I would use any extra earnings to reduce the mortgage, not buy a bigger house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels like a chance to make choices in daylight. I'd still be sad to leave the loader; I finally know its sounds well enough to notice when something's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you simply work until retirement in the loader seat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't rely on that. The robot date would find me at 56, and nobody has promised to keep a human operator on every machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the children to understand by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to see that learning doesn't end when you're older. I'd also want them to know I stayed at paid work for as long as I could, because a mortgage doesn't accept good intentions.

say: I'd tell the crew ten years should buy **paid training** before robots reach driving.
I'd say **planning work** changes in 2036, ahead of hands-on machines around 2039.
think: At **56** I cannot assume an operator seat or a secure retirement income.
The children would be grown, but the **mortgage** could still demand paid work.
do: Ask for funded **electrical maintenance training** next year if the mine offers it.
Keep operating while qualifying, then apply for **paid inspection posts** after 2036.
Use extra earnings to **reduce the mortgage** rather than enlarge the house.
feel: **Hopeful** about the time, and sad about leaving skilled driving.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a chance to make choices in daylight.
fieldNote: Her longer horizon reduces school costs but leaves a **mortgage** and an uncertain income after the robot date.
Yara values the loader's sounds and skill, yet names **paid inspection work** as a practical next application.

steps.text: Ask for funded electrical maintenance training next year if offered
Keep operating the loader while qualifying for other work
Apply for paid equipment inspection posts after 2036
Use extra earnings to reduce the mortgage balance

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the robot date follows so closely while I'm still learning the job. Paid course places and clear dates from the mine would help, along with a fair first chance at new posts. I can put in the work, but I need wages while I do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who covers the school pickup when a parent studies after shift. Dev can sometimes do it, but that's part of whether a course is possible. Training notices should say the hours, not just the course title.

headlineQuote: I can put in the work, but I need wages while I do it.
portrait: Yara is a **43-year-old junior miner** learning to operate a loader at a large mine.
She and Dev have two **school-age children**, a mortgage, and a few months of expenses saved.
She uses AI daily, wants a **union voice** on targets, and would study while keeping paid shifts.
Fast robots frighten her most; more warning lets her seek **funded training** and paid inspection work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves Yara little time before capable robots could replace her loader seat around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid course places**, clear dates, and first access to new posts would let her train without losing wages.
